sections.body: Everything discussed so far measures association: people who say this also say that. Business decisions usually need causation: if we change the price, what happens to revenue. The only method that answers causal questions cleanly is the randomised controlled experiment, and it is far more available to ordinary firms than most realise. The logic is simple and powerful. Randomly assign units — visitors, stores, mailing recipients, postcodes — to a treatment and a control condition. Because assignment is random, the two groups differ only by chance in every respect, observed and unobserved, so any systematic difference in outcome after treatment is caused by the treatment. This dissolves the confounding that ruins observational comparisons. If you simply compare customers who received an offer with those who did not, you are comparing people your targeting model already thought were likely to buy against people it did not, and the offer will appear miraculous. The practical constraints are statistical power and duration. Power is the probability of detecting an effect that genuinely exists, conventionally set at eighty per cent. For a conversion rate near five per cent, detecting a relative improvement of ten per cent — from 5.0 to 5.5 per cent — requires roughly thirty thousand units per arm. Detecting a twenty per cent lift needs about a quarter of that; detecting a two per cent lift needs about twenty-five times more. Because required sample scales with the inverse square of the effect size, small effects are extraordinarily expensive to measure, and most organisations quietly run underpowered tests that produce noisy, unrepeatable wins. Compute the required sample before launching, and if you cannot reach it, either test a bolder change or accept that you are not going to learn anything. Discipline matters more than sophistication. Fix the sample size and duration in advance; peeking at results and stopping when significance appears inflates the false-positive rate from five per cent to well over twenty. Run for whole weeks to absorb day-of-week effects. Test one substantive change at a time, or use a proper factorial design if you genuinely need interactions. Define the primary metric before the test, and treat everything else as exploratory; twenty secondary metrics guarantee one spurious significant result. Where randomisation is impossible, quasi-experimental designs offer partial rescue. Geographic holdouts withhold a campaign from matched regions. Difference-in-differences compares the change in treated and untreated groups, which removes any fixed difference between them, provided their trends were parallel beforehand — a testable assumption. Regression discontinuity exploits an arbitrary threshold, such as a loyalty tier cut-off, comparing customers just either side of it. Synthetic control constructs a weighted blend of untreated regions that tracks the treated one historically. All are weaker than randomisation and all rest on assumptions you must state, but each is far stronger than a before-and-after comparison, which confounds your intervention with everything else that happened that month.

sections.heading: Concept Testing, Prototypes, and Behavioural Signals
sections.body: Concept testing sits between a good idea and a costly build, and it is where stated-preference optimism does the most damage. The standard instrument is a concept board — a short written proposition with a visual, describing the benefit, the reason to believe it, and the price — followed by purchase intent on a five-point scale from definitely would not buy to definitely would buy. Norms exist by category, and the top-two-box score is usually compared against a database of past concepts rather than read in absolute terms, because respondents anchor differently across cultures and categories. The critical correction is calibration. Across consumer packaged goods, roughly a quarter to a half of those who say definitely would buy actually buy within a year, and the rate for probably would buy is far lower, often under ten per cent. Forecast models therefore apply weights of perhaps 0.4 to definitely and 0.15 to probably, then multiply by awareness and distribution assumptions. Any forecast that skips these multipliers is fiction. The most useful comparison is not against an absolute threshold at all but against a concept for a product you have already launched and whose real performance you know; that internal benchmark absorbs most of the systematic bias. Better still, replace what people say with something that costs them. A smoke test advertises the proposition and measures click-through and sign-up at a real landing page. A pre-order or crowdfunding page asks for money or a card detail. A concierge test delivers the service manually to the first customers before anything is automated. A Wizard-of-Oz prototype presents a working front end with a human doing the work behind it. Each converts an opinion into a decision with a real cost attached, and the drop between the two is usually startling. It is common for a concept with sixty per cent stated intent to convert at two per cent when a live page asks for an email address. Prototype testing then answers a different question: not whether people want it but whether they can use it. Jakob Nielsen's much-cited 1993 analysis argued that five participants in a usability test uncover roughly eighty-five per cent of the problems, because problems that affect many users are found immediately. The figure is a rule of thumb rather than a law, and it holds only within one homogeneous user group and one task set; with three distinct groups you need five each. Run tasks, not demonstrations: give the participant a realistic goal and stay silent while they attempt it. The informative moments are hesitation, misdirected clicks and the sentence I assume this does something. Never explain the interface during the test, however painful the silence becomes, because you cannot stand beside every future customer explaining it.

sections.heading: Analysing Qualitative Material Without Fooling Yourself
sections.body: Qualitative analysis has a reputation for softness that it does not deserve, and the reputation is earned mostly by people who skip the analysis and simply quote whatever they remember. Done properly it is a systematic, auditable procedure that another researcher could repeat on the same transcripts and reach broadly similar conclusions. The core method is thematic coding, and the practical distinction is between deductive and inductive coding. Deductive coding starts from a framework derived from the research questions and assigns passages to predefined buckets; it is fast and it answers the question you asked, but it cannot discover anything you did not anticipate. Inductive coding, associated with grounded theory as set out by Glaser and Strauss in 1967, works upward from the material: open coding labels every meaningful passage with a short descriptive tag in the respondent's own language, axial coding groups those tags into categories and relationships, and selective coding identifies the handful of themes that organise the rest. Most commercial work is hybrid, running a deductive frame for the client's questions and an inductive pass for surprises, which is where the value usually is. Discipline comes from a few concrete habits. Code from full transcripts or recordings, not from your notes, because notes already encode your interpretation. Keep a codebook with a written definition and an anchor example for each code, and note when you split or merge codes and why. Count the number of distinct participants who expressed a theme, not the number of mentions, so a single voluble respondent cannot inflate a theme. Actively hunt for disconfirming cases — the participants who contradict your emerging story — and account for them explicitly, since a narrative with no exceptions is usually a narrative that has been curated. Where the stakes are high, have a second person independently code a subset, perhaps twenty per cent, and compare; formal agreement statistics such as Cohen's kappa are often overkill in commercial work, but a structured conversation about every disagreement will find real ambiguities in your definitions. Report themes with three components: a plain statement of the pattern, a count of how many participants of how many showed it, and one or two verbatim quotations that illustrate rather than prove it. Quotations are evidence of texture and language, not of prevalence, and presenting them as prevalence is the field's characteristic dishonesty. Distinguish clearly between what participants said, what they did, and what you infer; three columns in the analysis document will keep the boundary visible. Triangulation is the strongest safeguard: a finding that appears in interviews, is visible in observation, and is consistent with behavioural data deserves confidence, whereas one that appears in only one source deserves a hypothesis marker and a plan to test it. Finally, keep an audit trail — the guide, the transcripts, the codebook, the coded extracts — so that when someone six months later disputes a conclusion, you can show them how it was reached rather than relying on institutional memory.

sections.heading: Analysing Survey Data: Weighting, Significance, and Segments
sections.body: Quantitative analysis begins before any cross-tabulation, with weighting. Almost no achieved sample matches its target population, so results are adjusted so that the sample's demographic profile matches known population benchmarks from a census or an authoritative survey. The simplest approach is cell weighting, where each age-by-gender-by-region cell is scaled to its true share. Where cells become too thin, iterative proportional fitting — universally known as raking, introduced by Deming and Stephan in 1940 — adjusts each dimension in turn and repeats until all marginal distributions match simultaneously. Weighting corrects the composition you can observe; it does nothing about the ways non-responders differ within a cell, which is why heavy weights are a warning sign. Inspect the weight distribution and be uneasy about any respondent carrying a weight above about three, since a handful of such cases can drive a whole result. Then compute significance honestly. A difference between two subgroups needs a test, and for proportions the two-proportion z-test is standard. As a rough guide, with two independent groups of 200 each, a gap of about ten percentage points is required for significance at the ninety-five per cent level; with 500 each, about six points; with 1,000 each, about four. Report confidence intervals rather than bare significance flags where possible, because an interval communicates precision while a star communicates only a threshold crossing. Adjust for multiple comparisons when you are scanning many cells: with fifty independent comparisons at the five per cent level, about two and a half will appear significant purely by chance, and a banner table with three hundred cells is a machine for generating false discoveries. Segmentation deserves particular scepticism. Clustering algorithms such as k-means or latent class analysis will always return segments, whether or not real groups exist, because partitioning is what they do. A segmentation is useful only if it is stable when you re-run it on a random half of the data, if the segments differ on behaviour rather than merely on attitude, and above all if you can identify which segment a real customer belongs to using information you actually hold. A beautiful six-segment model whose membership depends on twelve attitudinal questions you will never ask again is an artefact, not a strategy. Pre-specify a maximum number of segments and a typing tool before you begin. Finally, present with restraint. A survey estimate of 34 per cent is not 34 per cent; it is somewhere around a third, with an interval attached and unquantified non-response bias on top. Rounding to whole numbers, plotting intervals, and refusing to discuss changes smaller than the margin of error are the habits that keep an organisation from chasing noise for a quarter. When a tracking study shows movement, the first question should always be whether the sample composition, the panel supplier or the questionnaire changed between waves, because methodological drift explains more apparent trends in commercial trackers than genuine changes in the market ever do.

sections.heading: Ethics, Consent, Incentives, and Data Protection
sections.body: Research ethics is not a compliance overlay; it is a set of constraints that also happen to improve data quality, because people who trust the process answer more honestly. The foundations descend from the 1947 Nuremberg Code and the 1979 Belmont Report, which set out respect for persons, beneficence and justice, and are operationalised in market research through the ICC/ESOMAR International Code, first issued in 1948 and revised repeatedly since. Informed consent means the participant knows who is collecting the data, for what purpose, how long it will be kept, who will see it, and that they may withdraw at any time without penalty. Consent must be specific and freely given; a pre-ticked box is not consent under the European General Data Protection Regulation, in force since May 2018, and neither is consent bundled into unrelated terms. Recording requires its own explicit permission, and so does any onward sharing of video with a client. Where children are involved, most codes require verifiable parental consent below sixteen, and many national rules set the threshold at thirteen; check the jurisdiction rather than assuming. Data protection is now a genuine legal exposure. Under GDPR the lawful basis for research is usually consent or legitimate interests, and the principles of data minimisation and storage limitation mean you should collect only what the analysis needs and delete raw data on a stated schedule, typically twelve to twenty-four months. Pseudonymise as early as possible: separate the contact file from the response file, join on an arbitrary identifier, and keep the linking key restricted. Special-category data — health, ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation, political opinion, biometrics — carries stricter conditions and should be collected only when the research genuinely requires it. Penalties for serious breaches reach twenty million euros or four per cent of global turnover, which is a strong argument for a short retention schedule. Incentives raise their own questions. They must be large enough to respect the participant's time but not so large as to be coercive, particularly among low-income or vulnerable groups where a substantial payment can override a genuine wish to decline. Typical ranges are a few pounds for a ten-minute online survey, thirty to eighty for a ninety-minute group, and two hundred or more for a home visit or a hard-to-reach professional. Unconditional and prepaid incentives raise response more effectively than prize draws and are ethically cleaner because they do not gamble with the participant's time. Three specific prohibitions are worth naming because they are routinely violated. Never use research as a disguised sales approach, a practice known as sugging, which corrodes public willingness to participate in all research. Never present a respondent's identifiable data to a client without explicit consent for that specific disclosure. And never design a study whose findings you already intend to ignore, because that wastes the participant's time under a false premise, which is a real ethical harm even if no regulator will ever notice it.

sections.heading: Failure Modes, Limits, and What to Do When Research Misleads
sections.body: Research goes wrong in recognisable ways, and knowing the catalogue is worth more than any single technique. The most common failure is confirmation-seeking, where a study is designed, moderated and reported by people who already know the answer. The tells are a discussion guide with no questions that could produce bad news, a survey with no competitor in the choice set, and a debrief that opens with the conclusion. The remedy is procedural: have someone who disagrees with the expected result review the instrument before fielding, and write the pre-mortem forecast in advance so nobody can retro-fit their expectations. The second is the say-do gap, which is not a bias to be corrected so much as a permanent property of stated preference. People systematically overstate purchase intent, healthy behaviour, environmental conscientiousness, charitable giving, voting and exercise, and understate consumption of alcohol, sugar and screen time. Nothing in the wording fixes this; only calibration against known outcomes or a behavioural test does. Treat every stated intent number as a relative ranking device rather than a forecast unless you have a historical multiplier for that category. The third is the small-sample story. Two vivid interviews will beat a thousand-person survey inside any organisation, because narrative is more memorable than proportion. The countermeasure is to always present prevalence alongside the anecdote, and to be explicit when a finding is a hypothesis from four conversations rather than an estimate. The fourth is method drift in trackers, where a supplier change, a mode shift or an innocuous question rewording creates an apparent trend. Always overlap the old and new methods for one wave when anything changes, and report the bridge. The fifth is the limit of asking altogether. Customers cannot tell you about things they have never experienced; they can only reason from what exists. This is the honest core of the observation, variously attributed to Henry Ford and probably apocryphal, that people would have asked for faster horses. It is not an argument against research, which is how it is usually deployed, but an argument about scope: research is excellent at revealing problems, contexts, constraints and language, and poor at specifying solutions that have no precedent in the respondent's world. Ask about the problem, not the solution. When results contradict the plan, resist both instincts — capitulation and dismissal. Ask first whether the study could actually detect what you are claiming it found: check the base sizes, the intervals, the screening, the field dates. Then ask whether the finding replicates in a different method; a disappointing survey plus a disappointing live test is a signal, whereas a disappointing survey alone is a prompt. Record the decision, the evidence and the forecast in a decision log, and revisit it after the outcome is known. Organisations that keep such a log develop calibrated judgement within a couple of years and eventually need less research, which is the real end state of doing it well.

guides.title: Sizing a Market Opportunity
guides.summary: A practical guide to estimating how large a market really is, covering the TAM, SAM and SOM framework, top-down, bottom-up and value-based methods, data sources, sanity checks, the common ways sizing goes wrong, and how to present a number honestly.

sections.heading: What Market Sizing Is, and What It Is Actually For
sections.body:
Market sizing is the practice of estimating how much money is spent, or could be spent, on a particular kind of
product or service within a defined population and time period. The output is a number, usually annual revenue
in a currency, sometimes a unit count. It sounds like an accounting exercise and it is not. It is a
decision-support exercise, and the value of the work lies almost entirely in whether it changes what somebody
does. A founder deciding whether to spend three years building a product, an investor deciding whether an
opportunity can return a fund, a corporate manager deciding whether to enter a category, a lender deciding
whether repayment is plausible: each needs to know roughly how large the prize is before committing resources.
The word roughly is doing important work. A market size estimate is not a measurement, it is a model, and it
will be wrong. The honest goal is to be wrong within a band that still supports a clear decision. If a business
needs a hundred million in annual revenue to justify its cost structure and the market is credibly between
eighty million and a hundred and twenty, the sizing has failed to resolve the question and more work is needed.
If the market is credibly between two hundred million and two billion, the sizing has succeeded completely,
because either end of that range supports the same decision. Practitioners often say a good estimate is right to
within an order of magnitude, meaning a factor of ten. That is not an excuse for sloppiness; it is a statement
about what precision is achievable and about which decisions such an estimate can and cannot support. Two
distinct questions hide inside the phrase market size, and conflating them causes most of the errors in the
field. The first is descriptive: how large is the existing spend on things like this today. That is a question
about the present and can in principle be verified. The second is prospective: how large could spending become
if this new offering existed and succeeded. That is a question about a counterfactual world and cannot be
verified at all, only argued for. Established categories such as toothpaste or commercial insurance mostly pose
the first question. Genuinely new categories pose the second, and the honest answer usually involves reasoning
by analogy to a comparable category's historical adoption. When Uber was founded, the taxi market in San
Francisco was small; the relevant market turned out to be a much larger pool of trips previously made by other
means, which no descriptive estimate would have found. Recognising which question you are answering is the first
discipline.

sections.heading: TAM, SAM and SOM: The Three Nested Numbers
sections.body:
The standard framework divides the opportunity into three nested figures, and although the acronyms are
overused to the point of parody, the underlying distinction is genuinely useful because each answers a different
question. The total addressable market, TAM, is the annual revenue available if a single provider captured one
hundred per cent of demand for the product category, everywhere, with no competition and no practical
constraint. It answers the question of whether the category is large enough to be worth caring about at all. It
is deliberately unrealistic; nobody ever gets it, and a plan that assumes otherwise is not a plan. Its main use
is as a ceiling and a filter. The serviceable addressable market, SAM, narrows the TAM to the portion your
business model, product and geography can actually serve. If you sell a subscription in English to businesses
with more than fifty employees in the United Kingdom and Ireland, the SAM excludes consumers, excludes smaller
firms, excludes every other country, and excludes customers who will only buy through a channel you do not have.
SAM answers the question of how large the business could become if the current strategy worked completely. The
serviceable obtainable market, SOM, is the share of the SAM you can realistically win in a defined period, given
competitors, your sales capacity, your budget and the friction of switching. It answers the question of what to
actually put in a forecast. A worked illustration keeps the distinction concrete. Suppose you sell software that
schedules staff shifts. Global spend on workforce management software might be twelve billion dollars a year:
that is TAM. You sell only to restaurants and cafés, only in Germany, only to independent operators rather than
chains: perhaps 220,000 such businesses, of which realistically 60 per cent could use scheduling software, at an
average of 900 euros a year, giving a SAM around 119 million euros. You have four salespeople, a marketing
budget of 300,000 euros, and three entrenched competitors; in year three you might reach 1,800 customers at 900
euros, so a SOM of about 1.6 million euros, or roughly 1.4 per cent of the SAM. The three numbers tell different
stories and all three are needed. A large TAM with a tiny SAM signals a positioning problem. A healthy SAM with
a negligible SOM signals a distribution problem. Investors care most about TAM because it bounds the upside;
operators should care most about SOM because it is the only one they will be held to. Two refinements are worth
knowing. Some practitioners add a fourth layer, the total available market or served available market, but the
terminology is inconsistent between firms and arguing about labels wastes time; what matters is stating clearly
what each of your numbers includes and excludes. And all three figures are annual by convention. Quoting a
multi-year cumulative figure, or a lifetime value of all customers added together, inflates the number without
adding information and is treated by experienced readers as a warning sign.

sections.heading: Top-Down Estimation: Starting From Published Aggregates
sections.body:
The top-down approach starts with a large published number and cuts it down with successive percentages until
it reaches your segment. It is fast, it is the approach most people reach for instinctively, and it is the one
most likely to produce a confidently wrong answer. The method is straightforward. Find a credible aggregate,
such as national retail sales, total healthcare expenditure, or an industry analyst's estimate of a software
category. Then apply filters: the fraction in your geography, the fraction in your customer segment, the
fraction likely to buy your specific product type. Suppose an analyst puts global spending on cybersecurity at
215 billion dollars. Roughly 40 per cent is North America, giving 86 billion. Perhaps 12 per cent of that is
identity and access management, giving 10.3 billion. Perhaps a quarter of that is bought by mid-market firms
rather than large enterprise, giving 2.6 billion. That is your top-down TAM for mid-market identity software in
North America. The weaknesses of this chain are worth naming precisely, because they compound. Each percentage is
itself an estimate with error, and multiplying four estimates each accurate to plus or minus 30 per cent gives a
result that could easily be off by a factor of two or three in either direction. The starting aggregate is often
unverifiable: commercial analyst reports frequently cite one another in a circle, and the original methodology is
usually behind a paywall or simply undisclosed. Category boundaries are frequently drawn by vendors with an
interest in making a category look large. And a top-down chain cannot tell you whether any actual customer will
pay, because no step in the calculation involves a customer. There is a widely told story, probably apocryphal
in its details but sound in its lesson, of a business plan reasoning that the market for its product was
enormous because there are billions of people and if only one per cent bought it the revenue would be
extraordinary. The one per cent is doing all the work and is entirely unjustified. Any sizing where a small
arbitrary percentage of a very large number produces the answer should be treated as no estimate at all.
Top-down work has real uses. It is the right tool for a first-pass filter, for sanity-checking a bottom-up
figure, and for situations where the category is mature, well-measured by a statistical agency, and your
offering is a straightforward substitute for something already bought. It is the wrong tool for a new category
or a new business model. When you do use it, record every filter percentage as an explicit assumption with a
source and a plausible range rather than a single figure, because the whole value of the method later is the
ability to see which assumption the answer actually depends on. In the cybersecurity example above, the answer
moves by a factor of two if the mid-market share is 15 per cent rather than 25; it barely moves at all if the
North American share is 35 rather than 40. Knowing which lever matters is more useful than the point estimate.

sections.heading: Bottom-Up Estimation: Building From Units and Prices
sections.body:
The bottom-up approach reverses the logic. Instead of slicing a large aggregate downward, you count the units of
demand from the ground and multiply by what each is worth. The basic form is disarmingly simple: market size
equals the number of potential customers multiplied by the average annual revenue per customer. The work lies in
defining and defending each of those two quantities. Counting customers means identifying a real, enumerable
population. If you sell to dental practices, there is a licensing register. If you sell to farms above a certain
acreage, there is an agricultural census. If you sell to households with a particular characteristic, there is a
national statistical office. If you sell to construction firms, there are official business registers organised
by industrial classification codes, which in the United States is NAICS and in Europe is NACE. The discipline is
that you should be able to point at a list, or at a survey that measures the list, rather than at a percentage
someone asserted. Establishing revenue per customer means knowing what the thing costs, how often it is bought,
and how many units a typical customer takes. For a subscription this is annual contract value. For a durable
good it is price divided by replacement cycle, so a 900-pound appliance replaced every nine years contributes
100 pounds a year to the annual market. For a consumable it is price times purchase frequency. For a
transactional business it is transactions times take rate. Getting the frequency right is where most bottom-up
estimates go wrong, because it is easy to count who owns something and forget how rarely they buy another. Take
a worked example. You sell an inspection service to commercial building owners. The national commercial building
stock is 5.9 million buildings. Your service is only relevant to buildings above 5,000 square feet, which is
about 40 per cent, so 2.36 million. Regulations require inspection every five years, so 472,000 inspections a
year. Your price is 1,200, giving an annual TAM of about 566 million. Every one of those four inputs is
individually checkable and individually arguable, which is the whole point: a reviewer can attack a specific
number rather than dismiss the whole estimate. Bottom-up is slower, and it usually produces a smaller and less
flattering figure than top-down, which is precisely why experienced investors ask for it. When the two methods
are done independently and land within a factor of two of each other, confidence rises substantially. When they
differ by a factor of ten, one of them contains a structural error, and finding it is more valuable than either
number. One structural trap deserves special mention. If your product is bought by one party but used by
another, count the party who pays. Software sold per-seat but budgeted per-site, or a consumer product bought by
a parent for a child, will be badly mis-sized if you count users rather than purchasers, and the error is
usually an overstatement by whatever the average group size is.

sections.heading: The Value-Theory Method: Sizing by Economic Benefit
sections.body:
A third approach, less commonly taught but often the most illuminating, sizes a market by the value the product
creates rather than by what anyone currently spends. It is the right tool precisely where the other two fail:
when the category does not yet exist, when the product replaces an activity nobody buys today, or when the
current spend is an artefact of an obsolete way of doing things. The reasoning runs as follows. Identify the
economic pain your product removes, quantify it per customer per year in money, and then estimate what fraction
of that value a customer would be willing to pay for. That fraction is the price ceiling; multiply it by the
customer count to get the market. A concrete case makes it clear. Suppose you build software that reduces
unplanned downtime in factory production lines. There is no existing budget line called downtime reduction, so
neither top-down nor bottom-up counting of that category finds anything. But you can compute value: a mid-sized
plant loses perhaps 80 hours of production annually to unplanned stoppages, each hour costs roughly 25,000 in
lost margin, so the annual loss is two million. If your system credibly prevents 30 per cent of that, you create
600,000 of value per plant per year. Customers do not pay full value for anything; empirically, buyers of
business software typically expect to keep the large majority of the benefit, so a price capturing 10 to 20 per
cent of demonstrated value is the normal ceiling, giving perhaps 60,000 to 120,000 per plant. Multiply by the
number of plants of that size and you have a market that no analyst report contains. The method has two
disciplines that keep it honest. First, the value must be one the customer can actually see and measure. Savings
that are real but invisible, such as slightly reduced risk of a rare event, are notoriously hard to charge for.
Second, the value must accrue to the person with the budget. A product that saves nurses time creates real
economic value, but if the hospital's budget holder does not convert nurse time into money, the willingness to
pay may be near zero. This is the single commonest failure in value-based sizing: computing genuine value that
lands in a pocket nobody controls. The method is also the natural bridge to pricing, which is why it is worth
doing even when a conventional estimate exists, because it tells you whether your intended price is a small
share of demonstrated value, which sells easily, or a large one, which does not. A rough rule many enterprise
sellers use is that a product needs to demonstrate value of at least three to five times its price to be an easy
purchase; below three the buyer spends the whole evaluation arguing about the estimate, and the sales cycle
lengthens accordingly. The same arithmetic run in reverse tells you the maximum price a market can bear, which
is often a more useful output than the market size itself.

sections.heading: Where the Numbers Come From: Sources and Their Reliability
sections.body:
The quality of a market estimate is bounded by the quality of its inputs, so knowing which sources are
trustworthy, which are merely convenient, and which are effectively marketing, is a core skill. The most
reliable tier is official statistics produced by national governments and intergovernmental bodies. Census
bureaus publish business counts and receipts by industry classification. Labour statistics agencies publish
employment and wage data by occupation, which is invaluable for sizing anything sold per worker. Tax authorities
publish aggregate revenue by sector. Central banks publish payment volumes. The World Bank, the OECD, the
International Monetary Fund and Eurostat publish cross-country series with documented methodology. These are
slow, sometimes two or three years behind, and often use category boundaries that do not match how a modern
business thinks. But their methodology is published and nobody profits from inflating them. The second tier is regulated corporate disclosure. Listed companies publish annual reports with
segment revenue, and if a category has three or four dominant public players, adding their disclosed segment
revenue gives a hard floor for the market and often a decent estimate of the whole if you can find a credible
share figure. Industry associations publish surveys of their members, useful but skewed toward larger
firms. Regulatory filings, licensing registers, patent databases and property or vehicle registries are
underexploited and frequently free. The third tier is commercial research: subscription analyst firms and the
proliferation of low-cost market reports sold online. Quality here ranges from genuinely rigorous to entirely
fabricated. The warning signs of a bad report are recognisable: a market size quoted to four significant figures
with a growth rate to two decimal places, no stated methodology, a category invented for the report, and a price
of a few hundred dollars for what claims to be global primary research. Follow any widely cited number backward;
if the chain terminates in a press release rather than a method, discount it heavily. The
fourth and often most valuable tier is your own primary research: talking to fifteen or twenty actual buyers,
asking what they currently spend on the problem, what budget line it comes from, who signs, and how often they
buy. Twenty honest conversations routinely beat a five-thousand-dollar report, and unlike the report they also
tell you whether anyone wants the product. One caution on primary research: what people say they would pay is
notoriously unreliable, typically overstated by a large margin, so ask instead what they currently pay for
something comparable and what they had to do to get that budget approved. Past behaviour is evidence; stated
future intention is not. Two further sources are worth naming because they are often overlooked. Job
advertisements reveal what companies are staffing up to do, which is a leading indicator of where budget is
moving. And public procurement portals in most developed countries publish the value of awarded contracts, which
for anything sold to government or healthcare gives you real prices paid by real buyers, the single most useful
input a sizing model can have.

sections.heading: A Practical Procedure for Building an Estimate
sections.body:
Market sizing rewards a disciplined routine, because the errors that matter are structural rather than
arithmetical and a fixed sequence catches them. What follows works for most categories and takes a competent
analyst between half a day and two weeks depending on the primary research needed. Build it in a spreadsheet with one clearly labelled cell per assumption and no hard-coded numbers buried
inside formulas, so a sceptical reader can change one input and see what happens. Record the source of every
input in an adjacent cell, with a link and a date. Lead your presentation with the structure and the assumptions
rather than the answer; a reader who accepts your structure accepts your number. Keep the model on one page.
Complexity signals a question not defined sharply enough, and each extra assumption multiplies the uncertainty.
Expect to run the procedure twice; the first pass usually reveals you were sizing the wrong thing.
steps: Write down the decision the estimate must inform, in one sentence, and the threshold that would change it. For example: we build this if the obtainable market exceeds twenty million a year within four years.
Define the product category precisely enough that a stranger could classify any purchase as inside or outside it. Write the boundary down, including two or three explicit exclusions.
Define the customer: who pays, in what geography, of what size, by what channel. This definition produces the SAM later, so be specific.

Build a bottom-up estimate. Find an enumerable population of those customers from an official register or census. Establish price and purchase frequency from real quoted prices, not list prices. Multiply.
Build a top-down estimate independently, without looking at the bottom-up figure, from the best published aggregate you can find.
Compare the two. Agreement within a factor of two is fine. A larger gap usually signals a definitional error, and finding it comes before anything else.

Run a value-based cross-check: estimate the annual benefit per customer and confirm your price is a modest fraction of it. Above roughly a third of value created, expect a slow sales cycle and cut the SOM.
Narrow the TAM to the SAM using only the constraints of your actual strategy: geography, segment, language, regulatory approval, channel and product capability. State each explicitly.

Estimate the SOM from capacity, not from aspiration. Work forward from the number of salespeople or the marketing budget and a realistic conversion rate, then check the implied share against what comparable entrants achieved in their first three years.
Sanity-check the result against two independent anchors: the disclosed revenue of the largest incumbent, and a per-capita figure you can reason about intuitively.
Run a sensitivity analysis. Vary each assumption across a low, base and high case and identify the two or three that move the answer most. Those are the ones to research further.
Write the answer as a range with the reasoning attached, name the assumption it is most sensitive to, and state what would have to be true for the low case to be the real one.

sections.heading: Sanity Checks and Triangulation
sections.body:
An estimate that has not been checked against an independent anchor should not be trusted, and the checks are
usually quick. The first is the incumbent test. Find the largest company clearly operating in your category and
look up its revenue. If your TAM is smaller than the incumbent's revenue in that category, your TAM is wrong. If
your TAM implies the incumbent holds a 95 per cent share of a fragmented market, it is probably wrong too. Most
established categories have a leader holding somewhere between 10 and 40 per cent; a figure far outside that
range demands an explanation. The second is the per-capita test. Divide your market size by the relevant
population and ask whether the resulting annual spend per person or per business is believable. If you conclude
that every household in a country spends 400 a year on a product category most people have never heard of,
something is wrong. Conversely, if a critical business input works out at eleven pounds per firm per year, you
have probably missed a zero or mis-specified the frequency. The third is the substitution test. Ask what
customers spend today to solve the same problem, including internal labour cost, which is frequently the real
incumbent. If your product replaces two hours of an administrator's time each week, the substituted spend is
about a hundred hours a year at the loaded hourly cost, and any market size implying customers will pay
substantially more than that needs a story about additional value. The fourth is the top-down and bottom-up
convergence already described, done blind so that neither contaminates the other. The fifth is the growth-rate
test. If a source claims a category will grow at 30 per cent annually for a decade, note that this implies the
market becomes nearly fourteen times larger. Ask what has to happen in the physical world for that to be true:
how many factories, how many trained practitioners, how much regulatory change. Very high growth rates over long
periods are occasionally real and usually not. The sixth is the market share reality check applied to your own
forecast. New entrants in established categories very rarely exceed a few per cent share within five years; if
your plan requires 20 per cent by year three, either the category is genuinely new or the plan is fiction.
Triangulation is more valuable than precision in any single method, and two independent estimates that agree are
worth far more than one estimate carried to three decimal places. A seventh check is worth running whenever your
market involves a physical resource: count the bottleneck. If the service requires a qualified technician and
there are only 8,000 of them in the country, each able to serve perhaps 200 customers a year, the market cannot
exceed 1.6 million customers however large the demand, until more technicians are trained. Supply constraints
put hard ceilings on markets that demand-side reasoning never sees, and they are among the most reliable ways to
catch an inflated figure.

sections.heading: Segmentation: Why the Average Is Usually a Lie
sections.body:
A single market size figure hides the structure that actually determines whether a business works, because
markets are almost never homogeneous. Customers within a nominally single market differ enormously in how much
they spend, how urgently they need the product, how hard they are to reach and how likely they are to switch.
Averaging across them produces a number that describes nobody. The practical consequence is that the useful
version of a market estimate is a small table of segments, each with its own count, price and adoption
likelihood, rather than one line. Segmentation can be structural, by size band, industry, or geography;
behavioural, by how the customer currently solves the problem; or need-based, by which outcome they care about.
The most useful segmentations for sizing are usually the ones that correlate with willingness to pay. Consider a
market of 100,000 businesses. Naively, at an average price of 2,000, that is a 200 million market. Segment it
and the picture changes: perhaps 4,000 large firms would pay 15,000 each, giving 60 million; 26,000 mid-sized
firms would pay 3,000, giving 78 million; and 70,000 small firms would pay at most 300, giving 21 million. The
total is similar at 159 million, but the strategic implication is completely different, because the top segment
delivers 38 per cent of the value from 4 per cent of the customers and is reachable with a direct sales team,
whereas the bottom segment requires a self-serve product with support costs low enough to survive a 300 price
point, a genuinely different company. Two related distributions matter. The Pareto pattern, in which roughly 20
per cent of customers account for 80 per cent of revenue, is common enough in business markets to be worth
testing for explicitly. And the distinction between the early adopter segment and the mainstream, popularised by
Geoffrey Moore's crossing-the-chasm argument in 1991, matters because the first customers of a new category are
systematically unrepresentative: they tolerate rough products, have unusual pain, and are far easier to sell to
than the majority behind them. Sizing a market from the enthusiasm of early adopters is one of the most reliable
routes to overestimation. A useful discipline is to size the beachhead segment separately and treat it as the
number your plan must clear, with the wider market as the expansion story rather than the basis of the forecast.
A practical rule of thumb: a beachhead segment should be large enough that dominating it produces a viable
business on its own, and small enough that you can plausibly reach most of it with the resources you have. If
your beachhead is 300 customers and you need 1,000 to survive, the segment is wrong. If it is 400,000 customers
scattered across nine countries, it is not a beachhead at all, it is the whole market with a label on it.

sections.heading: Growth, Timing, and the Trap of the Compound Rate
sections.body:
A market size is a snapshot, and most decisions concern the future, so growth assumptions are unavoidable.
They are also where estimates most often become fiction, because compounding is not intuitive and small
differences in an assumed rate produce enormous differences after a few years. A market growing at 5 per cent
annually is 63 per cent larger after ten years. At 15 per cent it is four times larger. At 30 per cent it is
nearly fourteen times larger. Since the difference between 15 and 30 per cent looks small on a slide and
enormous in the outcome, any long-horizon growth rate deserves an explicit physical story. Ask what has to be
built, staffed, approved or changed in behaviour for the number to arrive. If a projection requires the number
of trained installers to triple, say so, because that is now the real constraint. Three particular traps recur.
The first is extrapolating a young category's early growth rate. New categories grow explosively from a small
base because percentage growth on a small number is easy, and the rate decays predictably as the base grows;
projecting the early rate forward is the commonest source of absurd forecasts. Adoption typically follows an
S-shaped curve, slow at first, steep in the middle, flattening as the addressable population is exhausted, and
the interesting question is always where on that curve you currently are, which is genuinely hard to know from
inside. The second is confusing market growth with your growth. A market growing 8 per cent a year does not lift
your revenue 8 per cent; you get that only by holding share, which requires effort. The third is ignoring that
prices in technology categories usually fall. Unit volumes can grow while revenue shrinks, which has happened
repeatedly in memory, solar panels, displays and data storage. Sizing in units and in currency can therefore give
opposite pictures, and you need both. Timing deserves separate thought. A market may be genuinely enormous and
simply not yet exist; being early is operationally indistinguishable from being wrong, because a company runs out
of money either way. The useful discipline is to identify what has to become true before the market opens, such
as a regulation, a cost threshold, an infrastructure rollout or a generational shift in habit, and then ask
whether that trigger is visibly approaching or merely hoped for. A market with a dated, external trigger such as
a compliance deadline is far more forecastable than one waiting for a change of attitude. One more caution about
published growth rates. A compound annual growth rate quoted over a long horizon in a commercial report is
frequently not a forecast at all but the arithmetic consequence of two independently estimated endpoints, a
current size and a target-year size, neither of which may be well founded. The rate then acquires an authority
it never earned by being quoted on its own. Whenever you see a growth rate, ask what the two endpoints were and
who estimated them.

sections.heading: Common Failure Modes and How to Recognise Them
sections.body:
Market sizing goes wrong in a small number of recognisable ways, and knowing the catalogue lets you audit your
own work and other people's quickly. The first and most damaging is the arbitrary percentage: taking a very
large number and asserting that some small fraction of it is achievable, without any mechanism explaining why
that fraction and not a tenth of it. Whenever the answer's magnitude is determined by a percentage nobody can
justify, there is no estimate present at all. The second is category inflation: describing your product as part
of the largest category that could plausibly contain it. A scheduling tool for cafés is not part of the global
enterprise software market. This inflation is often deliberate, since a larger number reads better, and it is
transparent to anyone experienced. The third is double counting, particularly in markets with intermediaries.
If you count the gross value of transactions flowing through a marketplace and also the fees the marketplace
charges, you have counted the same economic activity twice; decide whether your market is gross merchandise
value or net revenue and stay consistent. The fourth is confusing stock with flow. The installed base of a
product is not its annual market; the annual market is the replacement and new-installation rate. Counting the
whole installed base as revenue overstates by whatever the replacement cycle is, often a factor of five to ten.
The fifth is ignoring the alternative of doing nothing. In most business markets the largest competitor is not
another vendor but inertia, and a substantial share of the theoretically addressable population will simply
continue as they are indefinitely. The sixth is currency and inflation confusion in multi-year or
multi-geography estimates, which is unglamorous but routinely produces errors of 20 to 40 per cent. The seventh
is anchoring on the first number found, after which every subsequent piece of research is unconsciously
interpreted to support it; the defence is to build the bottom-up estimate before reading any published figure.
The eighth is motivated reasoning generally. If you need the answer to be large, you will find reasons for it to
be large, and no amount of spreadsheet rigour protects against a thumb on the scale. The practical remedy is to
write down the threshold that would change your decision before you start calculating, and to ask a colleague
with no stake in the outcome to attack the two assumptions the model is most sensitive to. A ninth failure is
subtler and worth naming because it cuts the other way: understating a market by defining it as the existing
category when the product genuinely changes behaviour. Sizing personal computing in 1975 by counting mainframe
buyers, or mobile telephony in 1983 by counting car-phone owners, would have produced defensible, rigorous and
badly wrong answers. The defence is not optimism but explicitness: state clearly whether you are sizing
substitution into an existing budget or the creation of a new one, and if the latter, name the closest
historical analogue and what its adoption actually looked like.

sections.heading: Consumer Markets, Business Markets, and Marketplaces
sections.body:
The mechanics of sizing change substantially with the type of market, and applying a business-market technique
to a consumer market produces nonsense. In business markets the customer population is enumerable. Firms are
registered, classified by industry code, counted by employee band and often listed by name in commercial
databases. Prices are negotiated but discoverable through procurement records and customer conversations, and
purchase decisions involve a defined budget holder. Bottom-up sizing therefore works well, and the useful unit is
usually the firm, the site or the seat, whichever the pricing model charges for. Watch for the distinction
between the number of firms and the number of buying units: a supermarket chain with 900 stores is one
negotiation and 900 installations, and which one your revenue scales with is the single most important thing to
get right. In consumer markets the population is known from census data but the behaviour is not. You cannot
enumerate who wants a product; you can only estimate a penetration rate, which is the weakest link in any
consumer estimate. The available anchors are analogous products' known penetration, survey data on stated
behaviour, and observed category spending from household expenditure surveys, which most national statistical
offices publish in useful detail. Frequency dominates in consumer categories: a product bought weekly at three
pounds is a bigger market than one bought once at a hundred. Marketplaces and platforms need a further
distinction that trips up many analyses. Gross merchandise value is the total value of transactions passing
through the platform; net revenue is only the commission or fee retained, typically somewhere between 2 and 30
per cent depending on the category. Both are legitimate numbers describing different things, and a platform
quoting GMV as its market size while comparing itself to companies quoting net revenue is not comparing like
with like. Two-sided markets also require sizing both sides, since the constraint is usually supply rather than
demand; a ride-hailing market in a city is bounded by how many drivers will work, not by how many people want
rides. Finally, regulated markets deserve special treatment because their size is often set administratively
rather than by demand. If a government reimburses a medical procedure at a fixed tariff and caps volumes, the
market is precisely the tariff times the cap, and no amount of demand-side enthusiasm changes it. The
compensation is that such markets are unusually easy to size accurately, since the tariffs and volumes are
published, and unusually predictable, since they change only when policy changes and policy changes are
announced in advance. Anyone sizing a market touching healthcare, energy, education, defence or utilities should
begin with the regulator's published schedules rather than with any commercial estimate, because those schedules
are the market. A related case is markets created by a compliance deadline, where the entire addressable
population is legally obliged to buy something by a known date. These are the most forecastable markets that
exist, and also the most competitive, because the deadline is visible to every potential entrant simultaneously.

sections.heading: A Worked Example From Start to Finish
sections.body:
Abstract method becomes clearer applied end to end. Suppose you plan to sell a compliance-monitoring service to
independent pharmacies in the United Kingdom, checking controlled-drug records automatically. Start with the
decision: you will proceed if the obtainable market exceeds four million pounds a year within four years. Define
the category: recurring paid software or service that monitors controlled-drug record compliance, excluding
general dispensing software and excluding one-off audits. Define the customer: independent pharmacy businesses,
not the large chains, in Great Britain, buying directly. Now build bottom-up. The pharmaceutical regulator
publishes a register of registered pharmacy premises, giving roughly 14,000 in Great Britain. Industry data
suggests around 60 per cent are independents or small groups rather than the major multiples, giving about 8,400
premises, held by perhaps 5,600 businesses since many independents own two or three shops. Pricing: comparable
compliance tools sell at 40 to 70 pounds per premises per month, so take 55, giving 660 per premises per year.
The bottom-up SAM is 8,400 times 660, about 5.5 million pounds a year. Now build top-down independently.
Community pharmacy in England receives roughly 2.6 billion pounds annually through its funding contract.
Pharmacy businesses spend somewhere near 1 to 2 per cent of turnover on IT, so call it 30 million across the
sector; compliance-specific tooling might be 15 to 20 per cent of that, giving 4.5 to 6 million. Two independent
methods landing within 20 per cent of each other is a strong signal. Value cross-check: the manual
reconciliation the service replaces consumes maybe two hours of pharmacist time a week, roughly 4,000 pounds a
year in loaded cost, so at 660 the price is about a sixth of the labour saving alone. Pricing is not the
obstacle. Now the SOM. With two salespeople each closing perhaps sixty
accounts a year, and referral growth, year four might reach 900 premises, or 594,000 pounds. That is well below
the four million threshold. The sizing has done its job: the market is real and the value case is sound, but the
plan fails on distribution, so the honest response is to find a channel, such as partnering with the dispensing
software vendors these pharmacies already use, rather than to revise the spreadsheet. Run the sensitivity
analysis and the picture sharpens further. Halving the price to 330 barely helps, since the constraint is
accounts reached rather than value per account. Doubling the sales team roughly doubles the SOM to 1.2 million,
still short. But a channel partnership reaching even a fifth of the installed base of one dispensing vendor
would deliver 1,600 premises in a single agreement, which clears the threshold on its own. The sensitivity
analysis has therefore identified not just the weakest assumption but the correct strategic move, which is the
best outcome a sizing exercise can produce. Note also what the exercise did not do: it never proved anyone will
buy. Every figure above is a count, a published price or a plausible rate. The next step is not more analysis
but ten conversations with independent pharmacists about what they do now and who signs.

sections.heading: Presenting the Number Honestly and Deciding What to Do
sections.body:
The final task is communicating an estimate in a way that supports a decision rather than manufacturing false
confidence, and this is where good analytical work is most often thrown away. Present a range, not a point. A
market estimated at 340 million invites a false sense of precision; a market estimated at between 250 and 500
million, with the base case around 340, tells the reader everything the first version did plus how much to trust
it. State the two or three assumptions the answer hangs on, with your confidence in each, and name the single
input whose revision would change the conclusion. Show the bottom-up build explicitly, because a reader who can
see population times price times frequency can evaluate your reasoning, whereas a reader given only a total can
only accept or reject it. Say plainly which parts are measured and which are argued. And be explicit about the
counterfactual: whether you are describing spending that exists today or spending you believe would exist if
your product succeeded, since these are different claims requiring different evidence. When the estimate is
finished, four outcomes are possible and each implies a different action. If the obtainable market comfortably
exceeds your threshold across the whole plausible range, proceed and stop refining the estimate, because further
precision cannot change the decision and the time is better spent building. If it falls short across the whole
range, the honest response is to change something structural rather than to re-run the model until it agrees
with you: raise the price by moving upmarket, widen the segment, change the business model so each customer is
worth more, or pick a different problem. If the range straddles your threshold, the sizing has genuinely failed
to resolve the question, and the correct next step is targeted primary research on the specific assumption
causing the spread, usually price realisation or adoption rate, rather than a general second pass. And if you
cannot construct a defensible estimate at all, which happens with genuinely new categories, say so explicitly
rather than producing a number to fill the slot. In that case the substitute is a cheap experiment: a landing
page, a pre-sale, a pilot with three customers at real prices. A signed order from one customer is worth more
evidentially than any spreadsheet, because it tests the assumption every sizing model rests on and none can
verify, which is that somebody will actually pay. It is worth ending on the limits of the whole exercise. Market
sizing tells you about the size of a prize; it tells you nothing about whether you can win it, how long it will
take, or what it will cost. Many businesses fail in enormous markets and some succeed handsomely in small ones,
because execution, distribution and timing usually dominate. Treat the estimate as one input among several,
revisit it annually as real customer data replaces assumption, and remember that the most useful product of the
work is often not the number at all but the understanding of the market's structure you acquired while
building it.

guides.title: Using Secondary Market Research Sources
guides.summary: A practical guide to finding, judging and combining information that other people already published in order to size and understand a market. It covers the main families of sources, how to evaluate them, how to triangulate a defensible estimate, and the legal and analytical traps to avoid.

sections.heading: What Secondary Research Is, and Why It Is Almost Always the Right First Move
sections.body: Secondary market research is the disciplined reuse of information that somebody else already collected, for their own purposes, and then published or licensed. It stands in contrast to primary research, where you go out and generate the observations yourself through surveys, interviews, focus groups, product tests, or controlled experiments. The distinction is about who did the collecting and why, not about how good the data is. A national census run by a government statistical agency is secondary research when you use it, and it is very often more accurate, more complete, and more carefully weighted than anything a small team could produce on its own budget. The word secondary describes provenance, not quality, and the single most common beginner error is to treat it as a synonym for second-rate. The practical argument for starting here is arithmetic. A statistically usable consumer survey with a few thousand respondents, professionally fielded and weighted, typically costs somewhere in the range of fifteen to eighty thousand US dollars and takes four to ten weeks from questionnaire design to clean data. Reading the equivalent published material costs a few days of one analyst's attention and often nothing at all in cash. Even when you fully intend to run primary research, the secondary pass is what tells you which questions are still genuinely open. Fielding an expensive survey to discover a fact that a government agency published for free eighteen months ago is the most avoidable waste in the whole discipline. There is a second, subtler argument. Secondary sources give you the shape of a market before you have any stake in a particular answer. When you interview twelve customers, you are already inside a story, and it is very hard not to hear confirmation. When you read three independent statistical series that disagree with each other by a factor of two, you learn something important about how contested the ground is, and you learn it before you have committed money or reputation to a position. Good analysts treat the disagreement between sources as information in its own right rather than as an annoyance to be averaged away. The limits are real and should be stated plainly at the outset. Secondary data was collected to answer somebody else's question, which means the definitions, the geography, the time period, and the population boundary will rarely match yours exactly. It is almost always older than you would like, sometimes by years. It tells you what happened, not why, and it is close to useless for anything genuinely novel, because nobody has yet had a reason to measure a product category that does not exist. The craft lies in knowing which of your questions the existing record can answer honestly, and being clear-eyed about the remainder.

sections.heading: The Source Landscape: A Working Taxonomy
sections.body: It helps enormously to hold a mental map of where published information comes from, because each family of sources has a characteristic strength, a characteristic blind spot, and a characteristic reason for existing. Sources do not lie at random. They are distorted in predictable directions by whoever paid for them, and once you know the direction you can correct for it. The first family is official statistics: national statistical agencies, central banks, and the international bodies that harmonise their output. This material is produced by law, on a fixed schedule, with published methodology and stated confidence intervals. It is the gold standard for population, employment, income, production, trade, and price levels. Its weakness is granularity and timeliness. A statistical agency will tell you how many bakeries operate in a county but will suppress the revenue figure if only two firms are present, because disclosing it would identify them. The second family is regulatory disclosure: what companies are legally obliged to publish about themselves. Annual reports, securities filings, prospectuses, patent applications, drug trial registrations, licence registers, planning applications, and lobbying disclosures all belong here. This is the richest vein for firm-level facts, because the penalty for lying is legal rather than reputational. Its blind spot is that it only covers regulated entities, so private and small firms are largely invisible. The third family is commercial syndicated research: firms that measure a market once and sell the same study to everyone in it. Retail scanner panels, television and digital audience measurement, analyst houses covering technology procurement, and the large subscription databases all sit here. The strength is that they measure things nobody else bothers to measure, at high frequency, with consistent definitions across years. The weakness is cost, opacity of method, and an incentive structure that rewards large and growing numbers. The fourth family is scholarly and technical literature: peer-reviewed journals, working papers, conference proceedings, dissertations, standards documents, and patents. This is where mechanism lives. If you want to know why a chemical process has a cost floor or how fast a technology has historically improved, this is the only place the answer is written down honestly. It is slow, often paywalled, and written for specialists. The fifth family is the trade press and what librarians call grey literature: industry magazines, conference presentations, consultancy white papers, think-tank reports, non-governmental organisation studies, and company blogs. It is timely, specific, and full of numbers that appear nowhere else, and it is also the least verified material you will handle. The sixth and newest family is digital exhaust: search-volume indices, web traffic estimates, app download estimates, job postings, review counts, shipping manifests, and satellite imagery. These are behavioural traces rather than measurements, which makes them fast and directional but poorly calibrated in absolute terms.

sections.heading: Official Statistics: Censuses, Surveys and Industry Classification
sections.body: Official statistics are the load-bearing wall of most market estimates, and learning to navigate them is the single highest-return skill in secondary research. The organising principle is industrial classification. In North America the system is NAICS, the North American Industry Classification System, adopted in 1997 to replace the older Standard Industrial Classification and revised roughly every five years. NAICS codes run from two digits at the sector level down to six digits at the most detailed national level, so 72 is accommodation and food services, 7225 is restaurants and other eating places, and 722515 is snack and non-alcoholic beverage bars. Europe uses NACE, the United Nations maintains ISIC, and most national systems map onto ISIC at the higher levels, which is what makes cross-country comparison possible at all. Product classification is separate: the Harmonized System, administered by the World Customs Organization, governs traded goods at six digits internationally with national extensions beyond that. Knowing the code for your market turns a vague question into a database query. In the United States, the Economic Census is conducted in years ending in two and seven and is the definitive count of establishments, employment, payroll, and receipts by industry and geography. County Business Patterns publishes annually with establishment counts and employment by county and NAICS code. The Bureau of Labor Statistics runs the Consumer Expenditure Survey, which tells you what households actually spend by category and demographic, and the Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics programme, which gives employment and wages by occupation and metropolitan area. The Bureau of Economic Analysis publishes the national accounts and, crucially for market sizing, input-output tables that show which industries buy from which others in dollar terms. Outside the United States the equivalents are the Office for National Statistics in the United Kingdom, Eurostat for the European Union, Statistics Canada, the Australian Bureau of Statistics, and their peers. At the international level, the World Bank's World Development Indicators, the International Monetary Fund's World Economic Outlook and International Financial Statistics, OECD statistical databases, UN Comtrade for bilateral merchandise trade, and FAOSTAT for agriculture cover most macro questions without charge. Two habits separate competent users from careless ones. First, always read the technical notes, because they define the universe: whether the figure counts establishments or firms, whether it includes the self-employed, whether it is at basic prices or purchaser prices, and what the sampling error is. Second, respect suppression and revision. Cells are blanked when confidentiality rules bite, so a zero may mean unknown rather than none, and most macroeconomic series are revised for months or years after first publication, sometimes substantially. Quoting a first-release number as though it were final is a common and avoidable embarrassment.

sections.heading: Company Filings and Regulatory Disclosure
sections.body: When a company is legally required to tell the truth about itself, the resulting documents are the most reliable firm-level data available anywhere, and they are usually free. In the United States, the Securities and Exchange Commission's EDGAR system holds every filing by every public company and many private ones that have raised registered capital. The annual report on Form 10-K is the centrepiece: it contains audited financial statements, a description of the business and its segments, a management discussion of results, and a risk-factor section that is frequently the frankest published account of an industry's structural problems. Quarterly results appear on Form 10-Q, material events on Form 8-K, executive compensation and governance in the annual proxy statement on Schedule DEF 14A, and the initial public offering prospectus on Form S-1. That S-1 deserves particular attention, because a company going public must justify its market to sceptical investors and therefore often publishes market sizing, unit economics, and cohort behaviour that it will never disclose again once listed. The segment disclosures are the market researcher's quiet gold mine. Accounting standards require public companies to report revenue and profit for their operating segments and, separately, revenue by geography and by major product line, along with any customer accounting for ten per cent or more of revenue. Assemble those segment lines across the six or eight largest players in a category and you have constructed a bottom-up revenue estimate for that category from audited numbers, which is worth more than any purchased forecast. Outside the United States the analogous registries include Companies House in the United Kingdom, which publishes accounts for private limited companies as well as public ones, the various European business registers, and the national securities regulators' equivalents of EDGAR. The depth varies enormously: a small British private company may file abbreviated accounts with almost no detail, while a German or French filing regime may demand more. Regulatory disclosure extends far beyond securities law. Pharmaceutical trial registries publish study design and results. Banking regulators publish deposit data by branch. Aviation authorities publish fleet registers. Energy regulators publish generation capacity and output plant by plant. Agricultural agencies publish acreage and yield. Telecommunications regulators publish subscriber counts and spectrum holdings. Environmental agencies publish emissions and permitted throughput, which can be reverse-engineered into production volumes for a factory. Lobbying and political-contribution registers reveal what firms are worried about. In most jurisdictions a freedom-of-information request can extract unpublished records held by public bodies, though the response time is usually measured in weeks to months and exemptions for commercial confidentiality are frequently invoked. The general principle is worth internalising: wherever an activity is licensed, taxed, inspected, or subsidised, a paper trail exists, and that trail is usually a better market measurement than anything anyone is trying to sell you.

sections.heading: Syndicated Research, Analyst Houses and Subscription Databases
sections.body: Commercial research firms exist because some things are genuinely expensive to measure and no government has a mandate to measure them. Retail measurement companies buy point-of-sale scanner data from thousands of stores and combine it with household panels who scan their own purchases, producing continuous category sales, price, promotion, and share figures at a granularity no public source approaches. Audience measurement firms do the same for television, radio, and digital media. Consumer-goods intelligence houses publish country-by-country market sizes across hundreds of categories. Technology analyst firms track enterprise software and hardware spending by vendor and segment. Financial data platforms aggregate filings, estimates, ownership, and transactions. Private-market databases track venture and buyout financings. These products are expensive, and the pricing is deliberately opaque. Enterprise subscriptions to the major platforms commonly run from the low tens of thousands to several hundred thousand US dollars a year; a single off-the-shelf industry report typically costs between two and six thousand. Access is often available at no cost through channels people forget: large public libraries and university libraries frequently hold subscriptions and permit walk-in use, national and state small-business development agencies sometimes buy seats for their clients, and industry associations occasionally bundle access into membership. If you are affiliated with any institution at all, check what it already pays for before you spend anything. The critical skill is reading these reports adversarially. A syndicated market number is a model, not a measurement, and the model has assumptions. Look first for a methodology section and see whether it names its inputs: a report that says it triangulated primary interviews with secondary sources and proprietary modelling, without naming any of them, has told you nothing. Look at the base year, because the historical figure is usually far better grounded than the forecast. Look at the definition of the market, which is where most of the disagreement between competing reports actually lives; two firms sizing the same category at four billion and eleven billion are usually not contradicting each other but including different things. Be alert to incentive. Analyst houses are paid by the vendors they cover through advisory retainers and reprint licences, and a large, fast-growing market makes for an easier sale in every direction. Forecast growth rates in commissioned reports skew optimistic with striking consistency. The correct posture is not cynicism but calibration: use the historical series, treat the compound growth projection as a hypothesis, and check whether last year's edition of the same report predicted the year that has now actually happened. That single check, comparing an old forecast against realised outcomes, will tell you more about a research house's reliability than any amount of reading its methodology page.

sections.heading: Scholarly Literature, Patents and Technical Standards
sections.body: Academic and technical literature is chronically underused in commercial research, and it is the only place where mechanism is reliably explained. If you need to know whether a cost curve can keep falling, whether a clinical benefit is real, whether a materials constraint is binding, or how a phenomenon was actually measured rather than merely asserted, the peer-reviewed record is where the argument was had in public by people with reputations at stake. Access is easier than most people assume. Google Scholar indexes nearly everything and surfaces free versions where they exist. PubMed covers biomedicine comprehensively and links to PubMed Central for open-access full text. arXiv hosts preprints in physics, mathematics, computer science, and increasingly economics and biology.
